name: Verdigris
poem: The green bloom of corroding copper — unstable, luminous, forever threatening to eat the very painting it adorned.

recipe.note: A bright blue-green teal, equal parts green and cyan, lifted with white.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: The brightest green available to Western painters for 1,500 years — and one that eats every layer of paint it touches.

entries.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
entries.blurb: Giovanna Cenami's gown is painted in glazed verdigris over lead-tin yellow — the green has stayed luminous for six centuries while the panel quietly corrodes.

entries.title: Egyptian Wall Paintings
entries.blurb: Tomb walls at Thebes are still vivid with copper-based greens — the pigment used to render papyrus marshes and the feathers of Ma'at.

entries.title: Madame X
entries.blurb: The famously scandalous portrait's brown-black dress was once a deep verdigris green — Sargent overpainted it after the colour started to oxidise.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Long before "teal" had a name, verdigris was the colour wealthy patrons asked for when they wanted depth — and could afford the maintenance.

entries.title: The Tudor Court Gown
entries.blurb: Verdigris-dyed velvet was the rarest greenwear of the Tudor period — sumptuary laws permitted it only to nobility and senior courtiers.

entries.title: Bottle-Green Wool
entries.blurb: Dark verdigris wool became the unofficial uniform of mid-century English country gentlemen — a colour deep enough to read as black at dusk.

entries.title: Tiffany Blue
entries.blurb: The exact verdigris of an oxidised copper rooftop — Tiffany chose it because turquoise meant value in Victorian iconography, and the colour was unmistakable.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Verdigris doesn't exist as a stable mineral — it's what copper does in the open air, slowly, over years.

entries.title: The Statue of Liberty
entries.blurb: Originally a polished copper orange, the statue oxidised to verdigris within twenty years — the green skin now protects the copper underneath.

entries.title: Tropical Lagoons
entries.blurb: The exact verdigris hue of shallow tropical water comes from sun reflecting off white sand through plankton-rich water — the colour of every postcard horizon.

entries.title: Patinated Bronze
entries.blurb: Verdigris on outdoor bronze is conservation gold — it stops further corrosion and looks reverent. Removing it accelerates the metal's decay.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: The colour reads as both luxury and time — it's why old money brands gravitate to it.

entries.title: The Tiffany Box
entries.blurb: Pantone licensed exclusively — the colour is so trademarked that even competitors mentioning "Tiffany blue" in marketing risks legal action.

entries.title: The Mint Green NHS Wall
entries.blurb: Hospital walls across the NHS were painted institutional verdigris — chosen for being calming, surgical, and proven to mask blood and rust.

entries.title: Mid-Century Kitchens
entries.blurb: Verdigris appliances — refrigerators, ovens, mixers — were the height of post-war optimism. Every kitchen showroom was a wall of "surf" green.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Verdigris is one of the few pigment names that's also a recipe — the word describes the chemistry.

entries.title: "Vert-de-Grèce"
entries.blurb: Medieval European colourmen called it "green of Greece" — the best verdigris was made by Athenian artisans who exposed copper to wine vapour for months.

entries.title: "Aerugo"
entries.blurb: The Roman name was admirably plain — "aerugo" simply meant the corrosion of copper, no metaphors. Roman doctors prescribed it as eye medicine.

entries.title: "Patina"
entries.blurb: The Romans called the green crust on their statues "patina" — from the small dish (patera) used in libations. The colour and the dish share the same oxide.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Verdigris has always been ambiguous — both poison and pharmaceutical, decay and beauty, weathering and wealth.

entries.title: Time-Made-Beautiful
entries.blurb: Old churches were never built to look verdigris — they were built copper. But the colour came to mean "old" in the best sense: weathered, sacred, intact.

entries.title: Poison Green
entries.blurb: Verdigris was prescribed for everything from warts to malaria — and was reliably toxic. Renaissance doctors didn't always distinguish between the two.

entries.title: The Green of Money
entries.blurb: The American dollar's verdigris-green ink was chosen as a security feature — early counterfeiters couldn't reproduce the exact copper oxide hue with cheap dyes.
